c.tagline: A desert oasis of merchant mansions, rosewater gardens, and one of the world's oldest ziggurats

card: International credit and debit cards (Visa, Mastercard) do NOT work in Iran due to sanctions — bring all the cash you need (euros or dollars to exchange) or arrange an Iranian prepaid tourist card in advance through a tour operator.

taxi.fare: Roughly $1-3 for a shared savari ride across town
taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before boarding for private taxis; shared savari taxis follow fixed routes at a flat per-seat price

emergency.note: Fire is 125. English-speaking emergency support is limited — a local guide or hotel staff can help translate

religion: small Zoroastrian and other minority communities historically present in the region
walk: The old city center around the bazaar and historic houses is compact and walkable; Fin Garden and the Sialk ziggurat are a short taxi ride from the center.

safety.safety: Generally safe for solo travelers, including women observing local dress norms; Kashan is a well-established stop on Iran's tourist circuit with a low crime rate
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare; standard precautions with valuables in bazaars apply. Travelers should stay informed on the broader geopolitical situation before planning a trip to Iran.

hood_landmark.Old City / Bazaar District: Kashan Bazaar and Agha Bozorg Mosque

hood_desc: The historic heart of Kashan, centered on the covered bazaar and the grand 19th-century merchant houses of Boroujerdi and Tabatabaei — the natural base for most visitors.
A quieter quarter around the restored traditional bathhouse, with several boutique heritage guesthouses converted from old courtyard homes.
The leafy southwestern edge of town holding the UNESCO-listed Fin Garden, Kashan's most famous Persian garden with its cypress-lined pools.

water.note: Treated but hard and salty in this desert region; most drink bottled water.

transit.sys: No formal public transit system for tourists; shared savari taxis and private taxis cover the city
transit.pay: Cash (rials), fare per seat for shared taxis or negotiated for private rides
transit.map: No formal transit map; ask your hotel for savari routes
transit.note: The historic center is compact enough to walk; taxis or Snapp cover Fin Garden and the ziggurat

transport.air: Kashan has a small domestic airport with limited flights; most visitors fly into Tehran (IKA) or Isfahan and travel onward by train or bus
transport.train: Kashan railway station sits on the Tehran-Isfahan main line, with up to 10 daily trains — about 1.5-2 hours from Tehran
transport.bus: Frequent intercity buses connect Kashan to Tehran (~3 hrs) and Isfahan (~2.5 hrs)
transport.ferry: None — Kashan is an inland desert city with no ferry service
transport.car: Reachable via Iran's main north-south highway between Tehran and Isfahan; a hired car and driver is common for day trips to the Maranjab Desert

airport.name: Isfahan or Tehran (Imam Khomeini) International Airport
airport.distance: Isfahan ~2 hrs by car/train; Tehran ~2-2.5 hrs by car/train
airport.transport: Train or bus onward from either city; private transfers can be arranged through hotels or tour operators

net.m: MCI (Hamrah-e Avval), Irancell, and Rightel provide coverage in Kashan; speeds are moderate and heavily filtered
net.w: Wifi is available in hotels and some cafes, though often slow
net.gb: ~$3-8 for a prepaid tourist SIM with several GB
net.fwn: Iran heavily filters the internet — Instagram, Facebook, Twitter/X, YouTube, and most Western sites are blocked; a VPN is essential and widely used by locals, though its legal status is ambiguous
net.ap: Buy a prepaid Iranian SIM at Tehran or Isfahan airport on arrival; foreign SIMs generally don't work due to sanctions

tip.s: Tipping (rounding up) is appreciated for guides and drivers but not obligatory
tip.r: 10% is a welcome gesture at restaurants where service isn't already included; taarof (polite refusal rituals) around payment are common in Iranian culture

places.name: Manouchehri House

places.name: Saraye Ameriha

places.name: Ehsan House

food.name: Baklava Kashani and rosewater sweets
food.desc: Kashan's diamond-cut baklava scented with rosewater and cardamom, alongside haji badam almond cookies and nan-e berenji.

places.note: Sweet shops in the covered bazaar sell baklava and rice cookies by weight.

places.note: Distillery village whose golab flavours most of the sweets; peak season is May.

places.name: Manouchehri House
places.note: Serves rosewater sweets with tea in the courtyard.

food.name: Sharbat-e golab
food.desc: Chilled rosewater sherbet, sometimes with basil seed or lime, made from the Qamsar roses distilled just south of the city.

places.name: Bazar-e Bozorg drink stalls

places.name: Fin Garden teahouse
places.note: Cool shaded gardens where rosewater drinks and tea are served by the water channels.

food.desc: Black tea poured from a samovar and drunk through a sugar cube, often with rosewater sweets; the rhythm of every Kashan day.

places.name: Timcheh-ye Amin od-Dowleh teahouse

landmarks: Fin Garden (Bagh-e Fin)
A UNESCO-listed Persian paradise garden of cypress avenues, turquoise pools and Safavid pavilions, famed as the site of chancellor Amir Kabir's 1852 murder.
Tabatabaei House
This 19th-century merchant mansion dazzles with mirrored stucco, stained glass and elegant courtyards, showcasing the pinnacle of Kashan's celebrated traditional house architecture.
Borujerdi House
Built for a wealthy carpet merchant in 1857, its sculpted wind towers and frescoed reception hall by royal painter Kamal-ol-Molk make it Kashan's architectural icon.
Agha Bozorg Mosque
An 18th-century mosque and theological school of austere beauty, its sunken courtyard, twin minarets and mud-brick dome glow golden in late afternoon light.
Sultan Amir Ahmad Bathhouse
A jewel-box Safavid-era hammam with turquoise tilework and a rippling turtle-back roof, whose domed skylights create one of Iran's most photogenic rooftops.
Kashan Grand Bazaar
Centuries-old vaulted lanes lead to the sublime Timche-ye Amin od-Dowleh caravanserai, whose light-pierced dome ranks among Persia's greatest bazaar spaces.
Abbasi House
A vast six-courtyard clay-and-straw mansion built for a glass merchant, its carved stucco reliefs and mirror halls reveal Qajar-era domestic splendour.
Tepe Sialk
One of the world's oldest known settlements, this 7,500-year-old ziggurat mound on Kashan's edge offers a haunting glimpse into prehistoric Persia.
Abyaneh Village
A day-trip-able mountainside village of red mud-brick houses and villagers in traditional floral dress, preserving ancient Persian customs beneath Karkas peaks.
Jameh Mosque of Kashan
Kashan's oldest mosque, founded in the Seljuk era atop a Zoroastrian fire temple, features a fine brick minaret dating from 1074.

dom.op: Raja Passenger Trains (Islamic Republic of Iran Railways)

train.note: No international trains. Kashan is a stop on the main Tehran-Isfahan-Yazd line, with trains to Tehran in about 3 hours and Isfahan in 2-3; the station is well outside the old town, so allow for a taxi. Services are less frequent than the buses. Book through a hotel or agent, as Raja's site does not accept foreign cards.

bus.note: No international coaches. Kashan's terminal has frequent VIP coaches to Tehran (about 3 hours), Isfahan (2-3) and Qom, run by Seiro Safar and Hamsafar. Buy at the terminal in cash. Savings taxis and local buses reach Abyaneh and the desert at Maranjab.

ferry.note: Kashan sits on the edge of the central desert with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Natanz
half.blurb: A Seljuk-era Friday mosque and a Sufi shrine complex with a conical minaret sit in this small town on the edge of the desert.

half.name: Qom
half.blurb: The Fatima Masumeh Shrine, one of Shia Islam's most important pilgrimage sites, anchors this religious center and seminary city.

full.name: Isfahan
full.blurb: Iran's former Safavid capital centers on a vast tiled square flanked by a royal mosque, a palace, and a covered bazaar.
